reading.rtitle: The Application You Do Not Send
paras: Every family argues about which university to choose, and almost nobody argues about how many places to apply to. That second question is the one that decides the year. A student who sends two applications is betting the whole year on two answers, and if both of them are no in April, there is nothing left to do until the following September. The cost of one more application is an evening. The cost of not sending it is twelve months.

Counsellors describe a list in three parts, and the parts are not equal. One or two are long shots, where you are honestly below what the university normally takes and you apply anyway. Three or four are matches, where you meet what the page asks for and the answer could reasonably go either way. And at least one is close to certain and affordable without a scholarship, because a list where every single place depends on money you do not have yet is not a list, it is a wish.

Ask any of them what students regret, and the answer is the same and it is never the application that failed. It is the one that was never sent, usually the long shot, and the reason it was not sent is almost always the same sentence: I would not have got in anyway. Nobody knows that. If you would regret not sending it, send it. And if a conditional offer arrives, treat it as a real offer from the first day, because a deadline that passes takes the place with it and no letter arrives to warn you.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B1 reading, written for this lesson from the published guidance of university admissions counsellors

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: If I get the offer in March, I will send the certificate the same week.
If I miss the deadline, there will not be a second chance this year.
If I had another year, I would apply to six places instead of two.
If I were you, I would find out what the number covers first.
I am eligible for two of the three, and the third one needs a certificate.
The full scholarship is a long shot, and I am sending it anyway.

listenings.text: The question I get every October is which university, and the question nobody asks me is how many. That second one is the one that decides the year, so let me start there. If a family applies to one or two places, they are betting twelve months on two answers, and if both of them come back no in April, there is genuinely nothing left to do until the following September. Now, a list has three parts and they are not the same size. One or two long shots, where you are below what the university normally takes and you send it anyway. Three or four matches, where you meet what the page asks for and it could honestly go either way. And at least one that is close to certain and affordable without any scholarship at all, because if every place on your list depends on money you do not have yet, that is not a list. And the last thing, which is the one I actually came here to say. In fifteen years the thing students regret is never the application that failed. It is the one they did not send, and it is always the long shot, and the reason is always the same sentence: I would not have got in anyway. Nobody knows that. If you would regret not sending it, send it.

I turned down a place at a university everybody in my school had heard of, with a partial scholarship, and for about two months people assumed I had been scared, or that my parents had said no. Neither of those is what happened. The scholarship covered the tuition and it covered nothing else, and the city it was in is one of the most expensive in the country. If I had taken it, I would have been working four evenings and a Saturday, and studying with whatever was left, and that is not the year I went there for. So I said no, and I said it early, which I think matters. What I would do differently is the list. Two applications is not a list, it is a coin, and I knew that in October and did it anyway. If I had sent five, I would have had something to compare. But the decision itself I would make again tomorrow with the same information, and I have stopped apologising for it in conversations.
